articles.title: SpaceX's Falcon 9 Phaseout Could Have Ripple Effect for Pilots
articles.summary: Company's plans to wind down its workhorse rocket may prompt delays and safety concerns for airspace users.
articles.body:
SpaceX has signaled that it will one day phase out its workhorse Falcon 9 launch vehicle for the company's much larger Starship rocket, a move that carries major implications for other users of the National Airspace System (NAS).

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote Sunday on social media that once Starship-the largest rocket ever built-is "flying reliably several times per week," it "makes sense" to allocate resources to the gargantuan spacecraft. That, Musk said, would mean "winding down Falcon [9]."

A source also told Ars Technica last week that the U.S. government plans to end commercial Falcon 9 launches after 2028 and use the vehicle only for a limited number of contracted missions.

Starship is likely still a few years away from reaching Musk's desired cadence. That will hinge on both Starship and its Super Heavy booster achieving full reusability, enabling quick turnarounds between missions.

But if or when Starship replaces Falcon 9, the larger rocket will carry with it larger restrictions on the NAS.

Launch operators such as SpaceX coordinate with the FAA to establish aircraft hazard areas (AHAs), which are disseminated via Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs) at least 24 hours before a launch either as a temporary flight restriction (TFR) or stationary altitude reservation. The AHAs are calculated based on a spacecraft's trajectory and debris dispersion data.

That means larger or less proven spacecraft such as Starship often receive larger AHAs. The latest Version 3 (V3) Starship and its Super Heavy booster stand more than 400 feet tall, designed to deliver 100 metric tons of payload to low-Earth orbit (LEO). For comparison, Falcon 9 is about 230 feet tall and maxes out at about 25 metric tons.

In addition, while Falcon 9 has launched hundreds of times with just a handful of commercial failures, Starship has suffered anomalies on about half of its 13 suborbital test flights.

AHAs vary by mission. In 2020, NASA required a 40 nm TFR for Falcon 9's Demo 2 mission, the first test flight of SpaceX's Crew Dragon spacecraft. TFRs for launches at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, a key Falcon 9 launch site, typically span 30-40 nm .

But they can be far larger. The AHA for Starship's ninth test flight in 2025 covered a whopping 1,600 nm , nearly double that of the previous mission. The FAA warned the restrictions could delay more than 175 flights by an average of 40 minutes.

Future Starship AHAs could restrict even more airspace. In February, the FAA published an environmental clearance report regarding SpaceX's request for new Starship launch trajectories from its Starbase launch pad in Texas.

The new routes would allow Starship to advance from suborbital to orbital flights by flying over portions of Florida. But they would also necessitate new AHAs. The FAA estimated that AHAs for Starship launches over Florida could impact as many as 8,800 commercial aircraft operations annually. Those covering Starship return trajectories over Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California could impact up to 4,400 operations annually. Each could require dozens of airway closures over the Atlantic Ocean.

SpaceX is building additional Starship launchpads and aims to expand operations beyond Texas to Florida's Space Coast.

In an October letter to the FAA, Steve Jangelis, aviation safety chair for the Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA), criticized the FAA's analysis of the new trajectories' impact on the NAS. Jangelis wrote that the agency "continues to ignore fundamental airspace safety and operational issues."

The FAA also activates debris response areas (DRAs) in order to safely clear airspace below a rocket's trajectory after an anomaly occurs. Starship Flight 8's DRA, activated after the rocket exploded, delayed 171 departures and diverted 28 flights, placing another 40 in holding patterns.

However, ALPA contends that these mechanisms are ineffective. Jangelis in October estimated that out of four Starship test flights that required DRAs, the agency activated only one of them within a required 6-minute, 30-second time frame.

That may have been because the FAA lacked information. The Wall Street Journal in December reported that SpaceX waited to alert the agency after Starship exploded in January 2025, with some air traffic controllers learning of the incident from pilots who witnessed it.

Either way, the FAA has warned pilots to use "additional situational awareness" when flying through AHAs. In a January safety alert for operators (SAFO), the agency advised pilots to identify alternate landing sites in the case of a diversion and stock enough fuel to get them through a prolonged DRA. The SAFO warned that spacecraft have potential for "catastrophic failures resulting in debris fields."

The rate of Starship anomalies is likely to decrease as SpaceX rapidly iterates the design. The company is known for accepting early failures as a tradeoff of future success. Falcon 9, for example, conducted 26 launches in 2020 but flew a record 165 missions in 2025, dwarfing competitors and accounting for the majority of FAA-licensed space activities. Falcon 9 anomalies are incredibly rare.

Starship, meanwhile, completed just five suborbital test flights in 2025 and has flown two so far in 2026.

SpaceX won't be able to ramp up Starship's cadence until it begins reusing the rocket and minimizing anomalies. But even if its record improves, pilots would face broader airspace restrictions and the potential for more severe consequences if something does go wrong.

articles.title: 400-year-old ‘vampire’ grave discovered in Poland
articles.summary: The wealthy young woman was buried with a sickle over her neck and a padlock on her toe.
articles.body:
The excavation of an over 400-year-old grave in Poland revealed a burial scene that, although macabre, was likely orchestrated in the hopes of protecting local villagers. In the town of Pień about 60 miles east of Kraków, archaeologists discovered the 17th century remains of a young woman interred with booby-traps to prevent her from returning as a vampire .

Researchers from Poland's Nicolaus Copernicus University described their findings in a study recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports . First discovered in 2022, Grave 75 contained the body of a 17 to19 year old woman who likely died sometime between 1620 and 1674 CE. DNA analysis indicates she possessed a rare maternal lineage that traces back to Scandinavia, yet remains almost nonexistent in more modern Slavic regions. Despite this genetic anomaly, examinations of her childhood teeth showed she was raised near Pień.

Archaeologists were immediately surprised by the scene inside her grave. Disrupted soil inside the burial plot suggests someone briefly dug up the body before it even finished decomposing. They then rearranged her arm towards the northeast, placed an iron sickle across her neck with the blade angled to her throat, and attached an iron padlock to her left big toe.

Both the sickle and the lock are traceable to historic folk rituals intended to combat supernatural or demonic forces. Archaeologists note that Polish-Lithuanian communities in the 17th century often blamed disease, famines, and other disasters on the recently dead—meaning this woman may have become a scapegoat for recent calamities.

However, she likely wasn't an ostracized peasant. Thin metallic threads composed of gilded gold and silver wires that were once part of a silk cap were found near her skull. The inclusion of such a lavish accessory indicates that the young woman came from a wealthy family, although fears about potential malevolent powers didn't stop people from taking post-burial precautions. Her status also appears to contradict hints about her health, since her nitrogen and carbon levels point to periods of malnutrition.

Meanwhile, a green stain on her neck and palate bones is likely tied to a copper-containing object or medical treatment intentionally placed deep in her mouth or nasal cavity near the time of death. Even the grave's location suggests that a wealthy life couldn't always guard someone against supernatural suspicions. The Pień cemetery where she is buried doesn't appear on historical maps, and its location outside the village near a crossroads implies it functioned as a false cemetery—a site reserved for a community's shunned individuals.

While grim, this scene illustrates the complex intersections between faith, superstition, community, and wealth within rural European life during the 17th century. But if it's any consolation, the falsely accused vampire at least got to keep her head .

articles.title: A blood moon, a SpaceX milestone, a spacewalk and Trump to honor Artemis astronauts: 4 space stories to watch this week
articles.summary: A packed space-news week brings a milestone SpaceX launch, a spacewalk, a near-total lunar eclipse and honors for Artemis II astronauts.
articles.body:
Fancy yourself an astrophile? The stars are aligning! This week is chock-full of space-related news, from intriguing celestial events to the honoring of astronauts.

These space-related events come amid an exciting summer for stargazers. This August, many parts of the world witnessed a solar eclipse , marking the first total solar eclipse visible in mainland Europe since 1999. The event — in which the moon moves between Earth and the sun, blocking some or all of the sun from our view — led to skygazing celebrations, though many cities, such as London, were only able to witness a partial eclipse. But if you're someone who gets giddy to witnessing unusual happenings around the moon, you're in luck: the United States will see a partial lunar eclipse on Thursday.

Here's a rundown of all the space-related stuff in the news this week.

On Tuesday, at around 5:30 a.m. ET, SpaceX launched a Falcon 9 rocket from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. Carrying 29 Starlink satellites, the launch is the 100th for the Falcon 9 this year.

Those along the East Coast could spot the illuminated exhaust plume following the rocket's launch. After completing its mission, the rocket's booster successfully landed on the company's drone ship, A Shortfall of Gravitas , which is stationed in the Atlantic Ocean.

Elon Musk's SpaceX describes the Falcon 9 as "a reusable, two-stage rocket" that is designed for the "reliable and safe transport of people and payloads into Earth orbit and beyond." Because the rocket is the first "orbital class reusable rocket," it allows SpaceX to refly the most expensive parts, reducing the cost of space missions.

Taking a literal trip to space may not be possible, but you can live vicariously through astronauts by watching a stream of them taking a spacewalk. NASA astronaut Anil Menon and European Space Agency flight engineer Sophie Adenot's Tuesday spacewalk, in which they installed a high-speed communications antenna on the International Space Station, is available to witness on YouTube . It ended Tuesday afternoon.

The spacewalk marks Adenot's second, after she made history on Aug. 18 by becoming the first French woman to participate in one. In total, that spacewalk lasted nearly six and a half hours. While the pair removed the failed antenna, they were unable to install the new one before running out of time, according to Space.com .

A partial lunar eclipse will be visible in the United States

There's no need for special protective glasses to watch this eclipse. A partial lunar eclipse , which will create a phenomenon known as a "blood moon," will be visible in North America, South America, Europe and Africa between Aug. 27-28 — though exactly how clear it will be depends on both your specific location and cloud cover. This time around, the central and eastern United States and Canada are particularly well positioned , as the moon will be high in their skies at the peak of the eclipse.

The eclipse begins when the moon enters Earth's faint outer shadow at 9:23 p.m. ET Thursday. The eclipse will peak at 12:12 a.m. on Friday, when more than 96% of the moon will be immersed in the darkest part of Earth's shadow. At this point, only a small sliver of the moon remains outside of Earth's darkest shadow, while the rest will appear red, copper or orange — giving it the appearance of a so-called "blood moon." The eclipse will officially end just after 3 a.m.

Trump is awarding Artemis astronauts a Congressional Space Medal of Honor

On Friday, President Trump is honoring NASA's Artemis II moon astronauts with the Congressional Space Medal of Honor. The ceremony, to be held at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, will recognize the significance of their April trip around the moon .

The Artemis II mission marked the first crewed voyage beyond low Earth orbit since Apollo 17's voyage in 1972, and the crew flew farther into space than any human ever has before. This mission, according to NASA, paved the way for future surface trips to the moon .

NASA's Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, as well as Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, will receive the medals following their week-and-a-half trip around the moon. The ceremony will be streamed on Friday.

articles.title: Clearway Energy wind farm and Avangrid transmission proposals selected for Aroostook County renewable energy push
articles.summary: The Maine Public Utilities Commission announced its picks on Tuesday for a long-planned Northern Maine renewable energy program.
articles.body:
The Maine Public Utilities Commission announced the winning bids today for the Northern Maine Renewable Energy Development Program: a new 800-megawatt onshore wind farm in Aroostook County proposed by Clearway Energy Group, and a transmission line to Haynesville proposed by Avangrid.

Details of the proposals have been kept confidential so far. Clearway Energy is one of the largest owners of renewable energy generation projects in the United States. Avangrid is the U.S. subsidiary of Iberdrola that owns Central Maine Power.

The selections mark a significant milestone in the yearslong push to build transmission infrastructure capable of delivering new, utility-scale renewable energy to New England's electric grid. The Public Utilities Commission previously chose different winners following a 2021 request for proposals, but the projects fell through in 2023 without being built as costs rose following the COVID-19 pandemic.

Avangrid's transmission proposal appeared to be the most viable within "a commercially reasonable timeframe," said chair of the commission, Philip Bartlett. The proposal won the bid in large part because it would use existing transmission corridors where the company has already secured rights of way, he added.

Clearway Energy's proposed wind farm depends on the transmission line being built.

This time around, Maine is working together with four other New England states. This multi-state procurement process is unprecedented, according to the commissioners.

"I've not seen anything like this in the United States," said Commissioner Patrick Scully.

Maine's share of the transmission line costs is expected to be less than 11 percent, and the projects are expected to create 2,500 jobs in the state during construction.

The program is also expected to benefit the climate. Wind tends to blow most strongly in the winter when energy costs soar as oil generators need to be brought online. Having this additional renewable energy on the grid is expected to reduce oil-fueled power generation by more than 10 percent, according to Commissioner Carolyn Gilbert.

"This both reduces emissions and increases reliability and reduces costs," she said.

The Public Utilities Commission still needs to finalize contract terms with the two companies, and then the projects will need to apply for the necessary permits.

The transmission line is required to have 1200 megawatts of capacity, so 400 megawatts will still be available after the Clearway wind farm is built. The commission expects to issue another request for proposals for generation projects in Aroostook County to use that transmission capacity.

articles.title: FDA approves first wearable device to monitor blood sugar, ketone levels
articles.summary: On Tuesday, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a device to continuously monitor blood sugar and ketone levels in people with diabetes.
articles.body:
Aug. 25 (UPI) -- On Tuesday, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a device designed to continuously monitor both blood sugar levels and ketone levels in people with diabetes.

The Libre Duo 10-Day Continuous Dual Glucose Ketone Monitoring System is the first of its kind to be approved in the United States -- both the first wearable device to monitor ketone levels and the first to combine monitoring of ketone and blood sugar levels, the FDA said. It's approved for those ages 2 and older.

"Today's authorization is a breakthrough for the safety of children and adults living with diabetes," said Dr. Michelle Tarver, director of the FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health. "Knowing that ketone levels are rising, and having that information in real time, around the clock, can be the difference between early intervention and a life-threatening emergency."

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that 40.1 million Americans live with diabetes. About 2.1 million of them have type 1 diabetes, which also makes it important to monitor the levels of ketone, an acid. The body creates this substance when, due to a lack of insulin, it uses fat instead of glucose to produce energy. Too much ketone can cause diabetic ketoacidosis , a dangerous complication.

"Early detection of rising ketone levels is critical," the FDA said.

Until now, the agency said, people had to monitor ketone levels with separate tests that only provided a single measurement at one point in time. The new system combines blood sugar and ketone tests and monitors them continuously. Readings -- and alerts in case of dangerous trends -- are sent wirelessly to a smartphone app.

The FDA previously granted "breakthrough device" status to the system, which is meant to expedite the device's development and review.

articles.title: ‘Robots Right Lane Only’ road sign leaves community baffled
articles.summary: The unusual sign is actually the product of a speculative fiction project imagining a future in which robots have taken on the bulk of labor and are demandin...
articles.body:
A strange road sign along a highway in Lexington , Massachusetts, has drivers and bikers scratching their heads.

"Robots Right Lane Only," the sign reads, along with an illustrated cartoon robot head and a directional arrow pointing to the right.

The only clue to the sign's origins is a sticker on the back that reads "Lexford Department of Robotic Affairs."

Betty Gau, the chair of the Lexington Bicycle Advisory Committee — which is responsible for putting up signs along the road's bikeway — noted the sign's appearance in May. The committee ultimately decided to leave the sign up because it was "amusing and clever and harmless," according to Boston.com . But still, the origins - and meaning - remain a mystery.

The committee likes the sign's message, which tells everyone to stay to the right.

"The bikeway is for everyone, there's a variety of users from tricyclists to walkers to runners, we want everyone to be safe, even robots, they should stay to the right too," Gau told the outlet.

The sticker on the back refers to a fiction project that imagines a combined town of Lexington and Bedford — hence the Lexford name — in the year 2075. The aforementioned "Department of Robotic Affairs" is the fictional agency that oversees "the registration, compliance, behavioral monitoring, and lawful decommission of all autonomous robotic units operating within the Commonwealth."

The project's story describes a world in which robots have largely taken over the world's share of labor and have started demanding equal rights. It tells of robot protests, demanding to be set free from the "tyranny" of the Department of Robotic Affairs.

The speculative fiction project touches on questions that ethicists and even the broader public are grappling with as tech companies, their boosters, and their deep-pocket funders insist that AI will change the face of labor, leaving the bulk of humanity twiddling their thumbs on the unemployment line.

John Basl, a Northeastern University philosophy professor who studies Artificial Intelligence ethics, spoke to Boston.com about the questions raised by the project and said he'd grappled with them earlier in his career.

"Early on I thought a lot about, could we create AI that was conscious, and what would that mean ethically?" he said. "Would we have obligations to it? Under what conditions? What kind of problems would that raise? Are we prepared for it?"

He said that it's unclear right now if creating a truly conscious AI is even possible, but said that if it did happen, humans would have moral obligations to it in the same way a parent might to a child.

"Once we create a being, let's just assume we create a being that has mental states kind of like ours, then we owe it the same thing we owe each other, and to treat it otherwise or attack it otherwise would be akin to racism or sexism," he said.

For now though, the sign is just a goofy picture of a robot head that is, intended or not, helping to keep bikeway users safe by reminding them to stay to the right.

articles.title: Mars Might Have Been More Habitable Than We Thought
articles.summary: A new study, with data provided by NASA's Curiosity rover, has shown that conditions for life were once possible on our second closest neighbor.
articles.body:
Mars has always been considered the next best choice for human life if we decide to colonize other planets. In fact, research into just how habitable Mars could potentially be has been underway for years. Although concrete plans for colonization are still a long way out, the research is promising, and a new tidbit of information is likely the biggest advancement we've had in years to understanding our future on the Red Planet.

It has previously been established that Mars could theoretically be capable of producing life through the existence of old water streams. However, a new study published in Nature claims that there is proof of water cycling through wet and dry periods of time. This was concluded by using NASA's Curiosity rover to analyze mud crack formations, which were deemed conducive to repeated cycles. Some of the cracks, scientists theorize, indicate that water cycles were prevalent for millions of years.

"That was really exciting to us," contributor William Rapin told Space in an interview. "It was an unexpected type of rock, something we hadn't seen on Mars before."

This admittedly sounds very scientific, and we won't blame you for not entirely understanding what this means. Thankfully, the findings of the Nature study can be summarized as such. Since the cracks in these structures appear to be deep enough to sustain water for millions of years in a seasonal manner, the basis of life creation was at one point organically possible. If life was able to generate and live in these conditions, this means the planet Mars used to be was likely more than capable of hosting humankind.

"So far, research has focused on the question of whether life arose on Mars," William Rapin added, "and now we can also look for traces of how might life have arisen on Mars."

Although more research is expected, it is unclear whether it has already started. It is also unclear what this means for the current state of Mars. What caused the sustainability of life on Mars to decrease? Can the circumstances be replicated? These questions and likely many more are still unanswered, and the answers we are looking for likely won't be found for a while. In the meantime, it's really cool that we have concrete proof that cycles of life have been proven to have existed on Mars.

articles.title: 'You just saved the video dish': Two astronauts complete spacewalk to replace ISS antenna
articles.summary: Astronauts Anil Menon and Sophie Adenot completed a 6.5-hour spacewalk on Tuesday, (Aug. 25), installing a replacement Space-to-Ground antenna on the outside...
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

"Houston, we have a working comm link again."

Thanks to the efforts of two astronauts, such a call is possible again using one of two Space-to-Ground antennas outside the International Space Station (ISS). The pair finished the replacement of a faulty dish assembly during a spacewalk on Tuesday (Aug. 25).

Anil Menon of NASA and Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency (ESA), who previously removed a faulty dish during a spacewalk on Aug. 18, installed a spare in its place and moved the broken assembly from a temporary to more permanent storage location along the station's backbone truss.

With Menon positioned at the end of the Canadarm2 robotic arm and Adenot traversing by handrails to join him, the two Expedition 75 crewmates first retrieved a spare Space-to-Ground Antenna (SGANT) from an external stowage position. Menon and the spare dish were then maneuvered to the Z-1 truss, where it was mounted and connected to the station's power and data systems.

Menon and Adenot then retrieved the faulty antenna, which they had stowed on the Z-1 truss during the prior spacewalk. Menon (on the arm) moved it to external stowage platform-3 (ESP-3) on the starboard side of the truss.

The replacement work became necessary after the SGANT ceased being able to track NASA's data and relay satellites , rendering it unusable, beginning last November. A second antenna has been in use since, continuing the transmission of voice and critical data, but this repair re-established redundancy to the system.

"On behalf of CAPCOM and I, we're going to count down like a bolt: '3, 2, 1… You just saved the video dish, you just saved the video dish,'" sang astronaut Anne McClain from Mission Control at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, parodying the The Buggles' 1979 hit "Video Killed the Radio Star."

"Oh my god, it is hard to top that," replied Menon, who could be heard laughing along with Adenot. "I want to thank the entire team on executing this complex, time-critical operation successfully."

Tuesday's spacewalk began at 8:27 a.m. EDT (1227 GMT) and was completed exactly 6.5 hours later, at 2:57 p.m. EDT (1857 GMT).

The extravehicular activity (EVA) was the 283rd in support of ISS assembly, maintenance and upgrades. It was Menon's third EVA, increasing his total spacewalking time to 19 hours and 20 minutes. It was the second time that Adenot worked in the vacuum of space, raising her time on EVA to 12 hours and 53 minutes after becoming the first woman and fifth citizen of France to perform a spacewalk.

This was the sixth outing from the International Space Station this year, the second EVA for Expedition 75 and the 98th spacewalk using U.S. extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuits at the station.

articles.title: U.K. heatwaves are baking the grass and revealing 300-year-old secret gardens
articles.summary: Severe heatwaves and droughts across the U.K. are scorching the grass and causing long-lost 18th-century gardens and flooded villages to reappear.
articles.body:
The severe heatwaves baking the United Kingdom are causing plenty of frustration for residents, but the scorching temperatures are providing an incredible silver lining for historians . As water levels recede and lawns bake under the sun, traces of long-lost historical sites are suddenly becoming visible.

Lisa Dowd of Sky News recently reported on the phenomenon, describing the newly exposed sites as "a time capsule that's been opened by this scorching summer."

The extreme weather is revealing history that spans centuries. In the East Midlands, the remains of the lost village of Nether Hambleton have emerged from the mud. The village was deliberately demolished in the 1970s to make way for the Rutland Water reservoir . Falling water levels during the recent drought have laid its stonework and building foundations bare once again.

The heat is also exposing intricate landscaping. At Hardwick Hall, an Elizabethan mansion built in the 1590s for the immensely wealthy Elizabeth Shrewsbury, the parched grass revealed the ghostly outline of former flowerbeds. Laid out in 1833, the beds were arranged in the shape of her initials, "E.S."

A similar discovery occurred at Chatsworth House in Derbyshire . The scorched South Lawn revealed the swirling patterns of the Great Parterre, an ornamental garden created for the 1st Duke of Devonshire around 1699. The garden was covered over and replaced with a new design around 1730.

A spokesperson for the estate explained that the grass planted over the former stone paths and flowerbeds has much shorter roots than the rest of the lawn. When temperatures spike and the ground dries out, that grass burns much faster, creating a temporary visual contrast that highlights the original 17th-century design underneath.

"The heat has had, I suppose you'd call it, a kind of X-ray effect on the ground, with more hidden history being revealed elsewhere too," Dowd reported.

At Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, hot, dry weather exposed the outline of a 300-year-old garden that was famously dismantled in the 1760s. Andy Mills, head gardener at the UNESCO World Heritage site , expressed his amazement to the BBC at the sheer scale of the discovery.

"The footprint of it has appeared out on the lawn, and it is absolutely fantastic. It's a huge structure, it's just massive. We know it's there, we know it's under the ground, we know the archaeology is there, and it's just one of those happy coincidences of this very, very hot weather that these things appear," Mills said.

The heatwave is uncovering more modern history as well. Aerial surveys detected the outlines of World War I practice trenches hidden beneath a golf course in Conwy, Wales. In Carmarthenshire, the outlines of World War II-era Nissen huts emerged at Dinefwr Park, where they once served as a military hospital and later as a prisoner-of-war camp.

While the heat remains incredibly uncomfortable, the parched grass is providing a brilliant reminder of the layers of history hiding right below the surface.

articles.title: Oregon study finds summer steelhead fish may need new habitat as Steamboat Creek warms
articles.summary: "Persistent low returns in recent years indicate clear signs of trouble."
articles.body:
Oregon researchers are focusing on a growing risk to one of the hallmark fish runs on the North Umpqua River.

Their work suggests summer steelhead rely on exclusive habitat in a single creek, and that creek is warming quickly.

A new study found that helping the fish may require more than defending that remaining refuge; it may also mean establishing additional habitat reserved for summer steelhead.

On Aug. 17, the Wild Salmon Center (@wildsalmoncenter) shared an Instagram post about the new findings.

The group highlighted the new research — published in Evolutionary Applications — on North Umpqua summer steelhead, a prized wild run with low returns.

As co-author Dr. Tasha Thompson, a conservation geneticist with Wild Salmon Center, explained, the study identified a key constraint: Summer steelhead need access to habitat that other runs cannot reach.

Wild Salmon Center wrote that "persistent low returns in recent years indicate clear signs of trouble."

The post noted that, within this river system, habitat of that kind is effectively limited to Steamboat Creek.

Summer steelhead need cold, protected places to hold through warm periods before spawning.

If the only reliable refuge continues to warm, the fish have a lower chance of adapting, leaving the broader population increasingly vulnerable.

The North Umpqua has long been known among anglers for its steelhead.

Healthy runs support recreation, local businesses, and the identity of river communities built around fish and waterways. What the study underscored is this population's reliance on a single creek, even as that creek warms rapidly.

That makes protecting Steamboat Creek the immediate focus, as it remains the sole key habitat for North Umpqua summer steelhead.

Holding onto that refuge and keeping it as cool and intact as possible could help sustain the run while other solutions are pursued.

The strategy outlined in the post was expansion, not just defense.

Thompson and her fellow researchers also considered ways to open up new exclusive habitat elsewhere in the watershed, including in restored reaches above Soda Springs Dam.

That kind of work could reduce the risk of concentrating a vulnerable fish population in one place.

"In the North Umpqua, however, this critical habitat really only exists in one place right now: Steamboat Creek, which is highly vulnerable to climate change," Thompson warned.

articles.title: A giant cliff that vanished billions of years ago may explain the mystery of Earthâs âmissingâ billion years
articles.summary: Science News: The Grand Canyon exposes roughly 2 billion years of Earth's geological history, but more than half of that record is missing. Geologists call the enor.
articles.body: The Grand Canyon exposes roughly 2 billion years of Earth's geological history, but more than half of that record is missing. Geologists call the enormous gap the Great Unconformity, a boundary where rocks representing more than a billion years of geological time are absent. The mystery has persisted for more than a century, with scientists proposing ancient erosion, tectonic upheaval and glaciation as possible explanations. Now, a study led by Thomas Gernon of the University of Southampton offers a way to connect those ideas: a colossal escarpment that may have formed across ancient North America as the supercontinent Rodinia began breaking apart around 800 million years ago. The researchers estimate the escarpment could have stood roughly 1 kilometre high and extended for thousands of kilometres. As it gradually retreated inland, erosion may have stripped away up to 8 kilometres of rock in places, leaving the ancient crystalline basement exposed. Later glaciation could then have removed additional material, helping produce the enormous gap preserved in the Grand Canyon today.How researchers reconstructed the Great Escarpment of LaurentiaThe study, titled Exhumation of Grand Canyon's basement along the Great Escarpment of Laurentia, was published in Geology. The researchers combined plate-tectonic reconstructions with models of landscape evolution to investigate how western North America changed as Rodinia began to fragment. Their reconstruction suggests that a major escarpment developed along the margin of the ancient continent Laurentia, which included much of what is now North America. The proposed escarpment extended across a vast area corresponding to parts of modern Arizona, Utah, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Missouri and Illinois, making it a continental-scale feature rather than a landscape confined to the Grand Canyon.Why a retreating cliff could erase more than a billion years of geological historyA major escarpment does not necessarily remain fixed in one place. Erosion gradually wears down its slopes while rivers transport sediment away, allowing the steep boundary between highland and lowland to retreat inland over geological time. The researchers argue that the proposed Great Escarpment of Laurentia behaved in a similar way. As Rodinia began breaking apart, tectonic forces created steep, elevated terrain that was particularly vulnerable to erosion. Over tens of millions of years, that erosion could have removed up to 8 kilometres of rock in some areas, exposing much older basement beneath it. That process could account for a substantial part of the Great Unconformity, but the researchers do not present erosion from the escarpment as the only process involved. Their model also helps reconcile the idea with earlier research pointing to intense glaciation during the so-called Snowball Earth period. A high, steep landscape created by continental rifting would have provided glaciers with terrain that could be especially effective at eroding and transporting rock. In this view, tectonic uplift and escarpment retreat created the conditions, while later glaciation helped remove and redistribute more of the exposed material.What the ancient escarpment may reveal about Death Valley and the surrounding landscapeThe researchers also identified features beyond the Grand Canyon that fit their reconstruction. Their model places Death Valley within a lower-lying basin associated with the ancient escarpment, where sediment could accumulate as material eroded from surrounding high ground. The proposed landscape would also have influenced drainage patterns and the movement of sediment across the continent as North America changed during the breakup of Rodinia. Those changes occurred hundreds of millions of years before the Colorado River began carving the modern Grand Canyon. The geological record preserved in the region therefore contains evidence of several very different landscapes occupying roughly the same area over immense spans of time: ancient mountains and escarpments, eroding highlands, glaciated terrain and eventually the canyon landscape familiar today.Why modern escarpments provide clues to a landscape that disappeared 800 million years agoOne reason the proposed ancient landscape is difficult to reconstruct is that the escarpment itself no longer exists. Researchers therefore looked to modern examples for clues about how such features evolve. Large escarpments in places such as South Africa and Brazil show how steep continental landscapes can gradually retreat through erosion over immense periods of time. Their modern behaviour provides a useful comparison for understanding what may have happened along the ancient margin of Laurentia. The study does not claim to have solved every aspect of the Great Unconformity. Instead, it offers a framework that connects several processes previously considered separately: the breakup of Rodinia, the creation and retreat of a huge continental escarpment, intense erosion and the later effects of glaciation. Together, those processes could explain how kilometres of rock were removed and why more than a billion years of Earth's geological record are missing from one of the world's most famous landscapes.

articles.title: NASA aims to put astronauts back on the moon by 2028
articles.summary: NASA is targeting 2028 to return astronauts to the Moon for the first time since Apollo 17. Here’s how the Artemis program plans to make it happen.
articles.body:
It has been more than 50 years since Eugene Cernan and Harrison "Jack" Schmitt walked on the moon , and NASA is now on an ambitious timeline to return astronauts to the lunar surface.

Humanity has not returned to the moon since the successful Apollo 17 mission , but NASA's Artemis program is ushering in a new era of lunar exploration.

The Clock Is Ticking On Spacex's Race To Mars

Building on the success of Artemis I and Artemis II, NASA has selected the astronauts for Artemis III — a critical test mission before Artemis IV, the mission aiming to send astronauts back to the lunar surface for the first time in more than half a century.

NASA continues to target 2028 for the first Artemis lunar landing, a timeline it has maintained since mid 2025.

This Spacex Test Could Pave The Way For Nasa's Return To The Moon

Here's a look at how prediction markets are sizing up NASA's timeline for landing astronauts on the moon.

Will Spacex Land Anything On Mars Before 2030?

With Artemis III planned as a demonstration mission in low- Earth orbit, NASA will evaluate one or both commercial human landing systems being developed by SpaceX and Blue Origin — Starship and Blue Moon — ahead of the next lunar landing attempt.

Nasa's Artemis Program: Paving The Way For Humankind's Return To The Moon And Beyond

The mission will carry astronauts aboard NASA's Orion spacecraft and test the critical rendezvous and docking operations between Orion and the commercial landers. The systems will be needed to carry astronauts from lunar orbit to the moon's surface during Artemis IV.

NASA hopes Artemis IV will mark the first step in a long-term return to the moon, helping lay the groundwork for sustained lunar exploration and future missions deeper into space.

Artemis V, a second lunar surface mission planned for 2028, would follow Artemis IV as NASA aims to establish a cadence of one moon mission per year.

Exactly when astronauts will return to the moon remains uncertain, but NASA's push to the lunar surface is a top priority.

The agency hopes the mission will mark the beginning of a sustained human presence on and around the moon, and serve as a stepping stone for future exploration deeper into space.

articles.title: Atlantic's largest-recorded adult white shark 'Contender' moves into cool Atlantic waters off Canada
articles.summary: Contender the great white shark, is catching attention for his latest move into the northern tip of the Bay of St. Lawrence off Canada into much cooler water...
articles.body:
Contender the great white shark is catching attention for his latest move into the northern tip of the Bay of St. Lawrence off Canada into much cooler waters.

This movement has scientists watching him closely and considering how these northern habitats are used by great white sharks.

Why Is It Called A Great White Shark If It's Not Actually White?

Contender is the largest male white shark ever tagged by Ocearch at over 1,600 pounds and 14-feet long when he was tagged.

This adult white shark was tagged in January 2025 between the Florida / Georgia border in the Atlantic.

Since his tagging, OCEARCH has monitored Contender's movements to help understand the behavior and migration pattern of white sharks like him.

They noticed that around the same time last year, Contender was in the Bay of St. Lawrence in Atlantic Canada before moving south for winter .

1,400-Pound Great White Shark Makes Big Moves As He Heads North Behind Other Sharks

"His repeated return tells us something important: this far-north habitat may be more important to white sharks than we once realized. And that's the power of satellite tracking," OCEARCH Senior Data Scientist John Tyminski said. "One shark's journey can reveal an entire network of habitats that we might otherwise never know was being used."

OCEARCH believes Contender could head into the Strait of Belle Isle if he continues on his current trajectory.

Tyminski said the Strait of Belle Isle is "an ecological gateway," which creates a nutrient-rich environment for sharks like Contender.

Watch: Sandbar Shark Swims Off Rhode Island Coast As Numbers Across New England Surge

Waters in this area are much colder than normal, but great white sharks are able to adapt to the sharp temperature difference, OCEARCH said.

Based on OCEARCH's Live Global Shark Tracker, Contender is one of the furthest-north sharks in the Atlantic currently.

Ocearch is a global nonprofit organization dedicated to researching and protecting sharks, whales, sea turtles and other ocean life, tagging these animals to track and study their migration habits and behaviors from afar.

To keep up with Contender and his movements, as well as monitor hundreds of other sharks and ocean animals, check out OCEARCH's free global shark tracker app .

articles.title: Is Maine finally about to make wind power happen?
articles.summary: For nearly two decades, Maine has tried to build utility-scale wind in the northern reaches of the state. On Tuesday morning, utility regulators brought that...
articles.body:
For nearly two decades, Maine has tried to build utility-scale wind in the northern reaches of the state. On Tuesday morning, utility regulators brought that vision a little closer to reality, choosing an 800-megawatt wind farm proposal and a 1.2-gigawatt transmission line plan from the bids it received earlier this year.

"I think we now have a pair of projects that are incredibly likely to be built," said Philip Bartlett, chair of the Maine Public Utilities Commission, during Tuesday's deliberations.

The commission was tasked with choosing both a clean-generation development for Aroostook County, along the Canadian border, and a transmission project that would shuttle the power to the rest of New England. The panel picked a plan for an onshore wind farm, proposed by developer Clearway Energy, and a transmission line proposed by Avangrid, the parent company of utility Central Maine Power. The selection of the wind project is contingent on the transmission line getting built.

The developments are expected to generate some $400 million in net benefits for Maine consumers over the life of the projects, and create more than 2,500 full-time jobs during construction. The wind farm could lower by 10% the amount of oil — one of the costliest and dirtiest fuels — burned in New England power plants in the winter, Commissioner Carolyn Gilbert said.

"Maine ratepayers are significantly better off for this effort," she said.

Maine set its first target for land-based and offshore wind in 2008. Aroostook County, a region with lots of open space and particularly robust winds, has long been the focus of these efforts. For years, however, these plans failed to get traction, largely because the region is so isolated from the rest of the New England grid. The cost and difficulty of building new transmission was a significant part of the reason previous plans fizzled in 2016 and 2023 .

This time around, Maine went into the process with the support of other New England states.

Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Vermont all struck an agreement to share the cost of the transmission line. Maine utility customers will pay for less than 11% of the total cost.

The six New England states are also set to share the cost of a second transmission project that will strengthen the connection between the planned wind farm and the rest of the region. In March 2025, at the recommendation of all these states' governors, Independent System Operator New England issued a request for proposals for transmission infrastructure linking central Maine to the rest of the grid. The grid operator announced its preferred project in July, and is now accepting public comments.

This level of cooperation is, perhaps, unprecedented, Commissioner Patrick Scully said during deliberations.

"I've not seen anything like this in the United States," he said. "I think this effort deserves national attention and provides a model for other regions to work collaboratively to meet common energy, climate, and reliability goals."

The region's other states also considered the bids for energy generation, though there haven't yet been any announcements about whether they will choose to procure power from the wind farm.

While environmental and economic development advocates are optimistic about the selections, they note that previous plans have floundered. There are still many more important milestones to come, including financing, permitting, and construction, said Francis Pullaro, president of clean-energy industry association Renew Northeast. Project planners may also need to navigate public reaction to the proposal. The last major transmission line built through Maine sparked an outcry that led to years of delay and more than $500 million in added cost for ratepayers.

The federal environment for wind-energy development is also more difficult than ever. President Donald Trump has eliminated tax credits for wind projects and directed agencies including the Defense Department to freeze permitting for wind, though courts have ruled against these moves . The attacks have been especially devastating for ambitious plans to build offshore wind in New England, raising the stakes of developing onshore resources in Aroostook and elsewhere in the region.

Still, Pullaro is already looking ahead. The 800-MW wind project will leave room for another 400 MW of power to travel on the new planned transmission line, and Aroostook has plenty of wind.

"We have a lot of untapped potential up there," he said. "I think there's a real opportunity here to keep the momentum going."

articles.title: Fact Check: FAKE McLaren Stunt Video Showing Car Crash Is NOT Real -- Made With AI
articles.summary: Is a viral video of a man climbing onto the roof of a moving car and then crashing into a truck real? No, that's not true: The clip originated from an accoun...
articles.body:
Is a viral video of a man climbing onto the roof of a moving car and then crashing into a truck real? No, that's not true: The clip originated from an account that publishes AI-generated content. The video contained inconsistencies pointing to AI.

The claim appeared in a post (archived here and here ) published on X by @BricxNews on Aug. 21, 2026. It opened:

This is what the video attached to the post looked like on X at the time of writing:

The 15-second clip claimed to document a fatal stunt: A driver climbs to the top of a moving car, but as he looks into the camera filming from another moving vehicle, his car crashes into a truck.

The video, however, was initially uploaded (archived here ) to the internet earlier that day by an account that publishes AI-generated content on Instagram. The original post displayed a disclaimer:

The clip reviewed in this fact check contained several hallmarks of AI. For example, at the moment of impact, the driver's arm seems to penetrate the back of the truck:

articles.title: New York buoy tracks drinking water reservoir conditions as water costs loom for households
articles.summary: When the quality of a drinking water source declines, utilities can end up paying more.
articles.body:
A five-foot buoy weighing 700 pounds floats in Otisco Lake, New York, and while it may seem unusual to passing boaters, its purpose has nothing to do with leisure on the water.

Powered by the sun, the device is intended to help safeguard a key drinking water reservoir and, ideally, prevent worsening lake conditions from driving up costs for New York households.

According to NNY360 , the Upstate Freshwater Institute placed the faded yellow buoy in Otisco Lake in June to measure conditions throughout the water column and send that information to Syracuse twice each day.

The effort centers on heavy nutrient loading that researchers say may be causing the reservoir to age faster than other Finger Lakes. When the quality of a drinking water source declines, utilities can end up paying more for treatment, oversight, and major repairs, with those added expenses eventually reaching customers.

Otisco Lake supplied 44% of the water moving through the Onondaga County Water Authority's system. Lake Ontario provided more than half of the region's water, while Skaneateles Lake contributed 3%.

Because Otisco Lake serves so many people in Central New York, residents and conservation advocates see the buoy as a needed step that should have happened sooner.

If nutrient pollution continues to worsen, utilities may need to devote more resources to keeping water safe and reliable. That can put pressure on both public budgets and monthly household expenses, as well as overall household values.

"People have put a lot of money and a lot of effort into their homes out here and the property values will be very heavily influenced by what happens with the quality of the lake," said Russ Holihan, a resident of Otisco Lake for more than six decades and a member of OLPA's advisory board.

Excess nutrients can accelerate a lake's aging process, contributing to murkier water and more difficult-to-manage conditions. In reservoirs used as drinking water sources, prevention and early detection are typically far less expensive than responding after problems become more severe.

Instead of relying only on periodic sampling, the system can collect ongoing measurements and provide a clearer picture of what is happening beneath the surface, NNY360 noted.

By collecting data twice a day, the buoy gives scientists a better chance of identifying trends tied to nutrient loading and shifting water conditions before they grow into larger problems.

County support for the monitoring program totals $64,000 over two seasons, funding that Onondaga County 6th District legislator Gregg Eriksen helped secure. That investment is relatively modest compared with the potential cost of treating a more degraded water source or paying for larger infrastructure responses later.

Better data can also help decision-makers identify the most effective ways to protect the lake, whether that means improving runoff management, refining treatment strategies, or prioritizing watershed conservation. The buoy is not a solution on its own, but it can help guide more affordable decisions.

Keeping source water cleaner can help utilities avoid some of the highest treatment costs, protecting both public health and consumer budgets.

The buoy's daily readings may help shape how the region keeps that water safe — and how much families ultimately pay for it.

Eriksen is confident data collected by the buoy will put OLPA in a better position to qualify for more funding down the road.

"That's what the real eventual hope is," he said, according to NNY360. "That this buoy can collect the data that's going to lead to more good things for this lake."
